Geopolitics & Diplomacy
• Ukraine says Starlink remains restricted despite claims of restored service, complicating air defense and frontline comms.
• Brazil’s razor-thin presidential runoff pits Lula’s legacy against a Bolsonaro heir, with markets and governance at stake.
• Serbia heads into a snap vote where a student-led movement hopes to loosen Aleksandar Vučić’s grip; meanwhile, a US envoy signals Washington is prepared for a long standoff with Iran as post-election scenarios are debated.
• Scrutiny intensifies around Trump-world allies and legal exposure, while Musk-world politics and potential SpaceX–Tesla merger talk add volatility to US tech-policy dynamics.
• Malawi’s opposition presses for answers on the president’s prolonged stays abroad amid domestic strains.
Why it matters: War, elections, and tech-politics crosscurrents are reshaping alliances, market risk, and governance from Eastern Europe to Latin America and Africa.

Armed Conflict & Security

• BBC reporting alleges Sudan’s RSF deliberately targeted hospitals, acts the UN says may constitute war crimes.
• South Korea invited North Korea to border military talks amid escalating deployments; US–Israel post-election options toward Iran are being openly discussed.
• Microsoft and researchers say China-aligned hackers used AI agents to exploit a ConnectWise breach and spy on thousands of companies.
Why it matters: Escalating flashpoints—from the West Bank to Sudan and the Korean Peninsula—coincide with cyber campaigns, raising risks of broader regional and digital conflicts.

• UK retail sales fell more than expected as households cut back; Heineken warned weight-loss drugs could sap alcohol demand, adding pressure on pubs.
Why it matters: Energy shocks and AI-driven capital flows are colliding with consumer weakness, reshaping market leadership and policy trade-offs.

Why it matters: Extreme weather, mounting climate mortality, and ecosystem risks are forcing governments to balance near-term energy needs with long-term resilience.

Geopolitics & Diplomacy.title: Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill
Geopolitics & Diplomacy.text: When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”What’s Your Ask?Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits. Mapping Your Way Into WashingtonCongress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and TechnologyThe House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls. Shortcuts to InfluenceEarlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”

Artificial Intelligence.title: Why AI Can’t Replace Engineering Teams
Artificial Intelligence.text: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written in partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free!If you’re an engineer, you may feel like your skills aren’t commanding the premium they once did. Many engineers have faced layoffs or restructuring. But even for those of us who still have jobs, something corrosive is happening. You may have heard some version of this:“ChatGPT answered that in five seconds. Why can’t you?”Or, “I made this app in a weekend. Why is our team taking so long?”I worked on a team where leadership said things like this directly to engineers. This was in 2024 and 2025, when the AI craze was in full swing and Claude and ChatGPT adoption was rising.Demo-Driven DevelopmentGenerative AI (and the marketing behind it) gives people the illusion that the work is simpler than it is. A working demo hides complexity, and once someone has a website that works, they may decide they no longer need engineers, or start to distrust the ones they do have. Some CEOs want to believe they can replace an engineering team with a few sexy prompts. Many companies also want them to believe this.That website works great in the demo—under specific conditions and without users with thumbs for fingers. Then it has to plug into a system with millions of lines of old code, satisfy legal requirements, meet accessibility standards, and be delivered in a complex deployment process.Thinking that writing code was the only bottleneck for deploying new software is like the Titanic seeing the tip of the iceberg and assuming there was nothing underneath it.What you can do about itEngineers have a unique position in the AI space, because you have the capacity to understand how these models work much better than the average person. Use this to your advantage.Learn how AI models work. If you can’t already explain that LLMs are probabilistic, what tokens are, or why training data matters, spend a weekend fixing that. You don’t need to become a full-blown AI researcher. A few fundamentals will put you ahead of most people making the AI decisions.Teach upward. Turn that knowledge into teaching moments for the people who lead you. Explain the limits of these tools, and why a demo and a production system are different animals. It keeps people from truly believing that a notebook full of prompts can replace an engineering team.Consider the criticism of today’s processes. Some of what we do has been treated as ceremony for too long. Be willing to say, “you know what, maybe you’re right, this process is too slow for the speed we can work at now.” Conceding that earns you the credibility to defend the steps that matter.I still believe that speed at the cost of everything else is harmful—but that’s a topic for another time.Find your voice. Engineers at the forefront of AI adoption need to push back and explain why we do things the way we do. Nobody else in the room is going to do it for us.Don’t chase (too many) shiny objectsYour goal, in my opinion, is to save your organization from buying into the hype so much that they chase the wrong thing. Our job, before and after AI, is building safe and useful products for human beings, and engineers are still best suited for that.—BrianWe Need to Embed Ethics Into Our Engineering CoursesThe need to educate engineering students about ethics and social responsibility is widely recognized, but today’s curricula often miss the mark. Three professors propose a new approach: adding ethics training directly to core technical coursework. Read more here. Entertainment.title: The First Fully Authorized Fleetwood Mac Documentary ‘The Chain’ Is Premiering in 2027
Entertainment.text: SummaryApple Original Films has revealed the title of its Fleetwood Mac documentary, the first ever made with the band’s full authorizationThe film gathers the perspectives of Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks across more than five decadesIts premiere lines up with the 50th anniversary of Rumors, the album that gave the documentary its nameApple Original Films has officially titled its Fleetwood Mac documentary Fleetwood Mac: The Chain, marking the first time the band has signed off on a film telling its story from the inside. Directed by Frank Marshall, the project centers the five members of the band’s best-known lineup and is set for a global debut on Apple TV early next year.The documentary is built around the band itself rather than outside commentators. Mick Fleetwood, John McVie, Christine McVie, Lindsey Buckingham and Stevie Nicks, all Grammy winners and Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees, look back on the 50-plus years that followed their chance meeting in 1974. Archival material that has never been made public sits alongside exclusive new interviews, carrying the story from their record-breaking studio sessions and tours up to the present day.The title is a deliberate choice. “The Chain” is the only track on Rumors that credits all five members as writers, and the film uses it as a symbol for a bond that held even as the band’s rise to fame strained nearly every relationship within it. Timing reinforces the point, with the premiere landing on the 50th anniversary of the Grammy-winning album’s release.Structurally, the film moves through the band’s peaks and collapses while isolating what each member contributed to a sound that has sold more than 220 million records worldwide. It also digs into the harder question of why five artists kept returning to one another, and kept producing landmark work, despite pressures from the industry and from within the group that repeatedly threatened to end it.Behind the camera, Marshall, a five-time Academy Award nominee and recipient of the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award, also produces through The Kennedy/Marshall Company. He’s joined by White Horse Pictures’ Nigel Sinclair (No Direction Home: Bob Dylan), Nicholas Ferrall (Stax: Soulsville U.S.A.) and Jeanne Elfant Festa (Lucy and Desi), along with Kennedy/Marshall’s Aly Parker (The Bee Gees: How Can You Mend a Broken Heart). Cassidy Hartmann of White Horse and Tony Rosenthal of Kennedy/Marshall serve as executive producers, while Diamond Docs’ Mark Monroe writes and executive produces.Fleetwood Mac: The Chain premieres globally on Apple TV on Friday, January 29, 2027.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Chris Pratt Confirms Star-Lord Will Return to the MCU
Entertainment.text: SummaryChris Pratt has confirmed that Star-Lord will return to the Marvel Cinematic UniverseThe actor revealed on The Playlist’s Bingeworthy podcast that hard action has been taken by Marvel Studios leadershipPratt previously pitched his own creative vision to Kevin Feige to help shape future MCU storytellingMarvel Studios and actor Chris Pratt are officially moving forward with Star-Lord's return to the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Pratt confirmed on The Playlist’s “Bingeworthy” podcast that concrete steps have been initiated to follow up on the character’s future teased at the close of Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3.Speaking on the podcast, Pratt addressed his ongoing communication with executive leadership regarding Peter Quill's return, "I have a great relationship with Kevin [Feige] and Lou [D’Esposito], and there have been both ongoing conversations about how we make good on that promise and also hard action taken to make sure that we make good on that promise," said Pratt. He continued, "So yeah, you’ll see Star-Lord again, which is very exciting, but I’m not at liberty to say when that’s going to be, but he’s not going anywhere."The confirmation builds upon statements Pratt made earlier on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, where he admitted to pitching a concept directly to Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige. “I’m happy to do anything they want me to do and will,” Pratt previously explained. “And also, I personally have a really strong vision of what I would want him to do. And I think it’s fucking great.” When asked about bringing that proposal to Feige, Pratt stated, “Yep. And I think that, you know, I’m down to contribute any way I can to them setting up the next 10 years of storytelling, you know? And also, I have a pretty strong idea of how I think I could contribute to that.”Pratt has portrayed Star-Lord across six films to date, including Guardians of the Galaxy, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2, Avengers: Infinity War, Avengers: Endgame, Thor: Love and Thunder, and Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3.The next installment in the MCU, Avengers: Doomsday, is scheduled to arrive in theaters on December 18.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: LISA’s ‘PRESS PLAY’ EP Plays Out Like a Six-Track Action Movie
Entertainment.text: SummaryLISA has released 'PRESS PLAY,' a six-track EP conceived to unfold like a film from start to finishThe track “Tarantino” lands with a music video that sends LISA brawling through a hotel to reach her favorite directorThe drop sets up her VIVA LA LISA residency at Caesars Palace, the first Las Vegas residency by a K-pop artistLISA has officially released PRESS PLAY, a six-track EP built around a cinematic concept that asks listeners to settle in and hit play as if a movie were about to start. The project arrives today alongside a music video for focus track “Tarantino,” capping a run that has already delivered a record-breaking YouTube debut, a historic VMA win and a sold-out Las Vegas booking.The film framing shapes how the EP is sequenced, with six tracks moving like scenes rather than a loose collection of singles. “SaWaDiKa” opens the reel, followed by “V12” and “Cobra,” before “Tarantino” lands as the centerpiece and “Cut U Off” and “Sweat” carry things to the closing credits.“Tarantino” gets the blockbuster treatment on screen. Its video follows LISA on a mission through a hotel to hand-deliver a note to the director himself, throwing punches at anyone standing between her and the delivery. The action-heavy choreography leans straight into the genre the track is named after, making it the clearest visual statement of the EP’s movie concept.The project’s opener already arrived with serious numbers. “SaWaDiKa,” named after the Thai greeting for “hello,” came with a video shot in LISA’s hometown of Bangkok that pulled in more than 70.8 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours. That tally places it among her biggest YouTube debuts and makes it the top YouTube debut of 2026, while the song entered the Billboard Hot 100 at No. 69 for her highest debut on the chart to date. She gave the track its television debut at the MTV VMAs, where she also won Best Pop for “Dream” featuring Kentaro Sakaguchi and became the first solo K-pop artist to take the category.Las Vegas is the next stop on the rollout. LISA’s “VIVA LA LISA” Residency takes over The Colosseum at Caesars Palace for six nights in November, after the first four shows sold out in under 10 minutes and two more dates were added. The run makes her the first K-pop artist to headline a Las Vegas residency.Her story is also playing out on the big screen. Always Lalisa, a feature documentary directed by Sue Kim, is now in cinemas worldwide following its Toronto Film Festival premiere, tracing her breakout solo year around the release of Alter Ego, the launch of LLOUD and her solo Coachella debut.Stream PRESS PLAY on Spotify and Apple Music, and stream the “Tarantino” visual above.Read more at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Denzel Washington and Christopher McQuarrie Set to Team up for Untitled Amazon MGM Thriller
Entertainment.text: SummaryDenzel Washington is set to headline an untitled original thriller directed by Christopher McQuarrieAmazon MGM and United Artists have slated the feature for an October 1, 2027 theatrical releaseWritten by Scott Barkan and Gregg Zehentner the plot centers on a terminally ill ex-detective confronting his pastAmazon MGM Studios and United Artists have officially greenlit an untitled original thriller starring two-time Academy Award winner Denzel Washington and directed by Christopher McQuarrie. The high-profile feature is currently slated to arrive in theaters in the fall of 2027.Penned by screenwriters Scott Barkan and Gregg Zehentner, the project—previously developed under the working title The Frame—focuses on a former police detective who receives an early release from prison following a terminal brain cancer diagnosis. Hoping to spend his remaining time reconnecting with his family, he quickly discovers that his unresolved past refuses to stay buried.The collaboration with McQuarrie marks one of two major Washington-led productions scheduled for the near future. The actor was previously set to debut The Take—originally titled Here Comes the Flood and co-starring Robert Pattinson—before the end of 2026, though that production has since seen its release window pushed into 2027.The untitled Christopher McQuarrie thriller starring Denzel Washington is scheduled for a theatrical rollout on October 1, 2027.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The Nike Air Force 1 ‘01 “Philly” Gives LeBron James a Sixers-Coded Welcome
Entertainment.text: Name: Nike Air Force 1 ’01 “Philly”Colorway: White/Rush Blue-University RedSKU: JW9694-100MSRP: $140 USDRelease Date: Available nowWhere to Buy: SNKRSNike is greeting LeBron James’ move to Philadelphia with the Air Force 1 ‘01 “Philly,” a city-dedicated pair dressed in Sixers colors and loaded with local references. Rather than a signature-line release, the brand is leaning on its most recognizable low-top to mark the moment, building the shoe around Philadelphia itself.This is the second time in 2026 that Nike has turned the Air Force 1 ‘01 into a snapshot of a city’s basketball mood. Earlier this year, the “NYC” edition arrived as the Knicks pushed through the playoffs, its insoles printed with a pixelated rendering of Madison Square Garden. The “Philly” pair trades arena imagery for team colors and civic shorthand, keeping the tribute rooted in the city rather than a single building.Up top, the White/Rush Blue-University Red colorway is mapped with clear intent. White leather handles the toe, lacing area and heel, while royal blue covers the perforated toe box and side panels. Red leather Swooshes sweep across each side, and a smaller red Swoosh sits just below the laces to carry the accent color toward the center of the shoe.The heel is where the city really announces itself. One shoe is embroidered with “215” and the other with “PHL,” each outlined in blue and cut through by a red Swoosh, while white “Phila” lettering stands in for standard branding on the blue heel tabs. “215” is one of Philadelphia’s area codes, giving the pair a local detail only the city would fully read.Underfoot, a white midsole carries blue “AIR” lettering and sits on a blue rubber outsole. The most pointed detail hides inside: the insoles show a black-and-white brick wall split by cracks, with a red Nike logo smashing through one section. For a shoe built around a star landing in a new city, it’s a fitting image to stand on.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

The researchers were primarily investigating a population of neurons found in the hippocampus, involved in memory function, but find that the gene is relevant in supporting cells of the brain also, such as microglia. Expression of PLA2G2F increases with age, and artificially increasing expression over natural levels produces greater protection. Longevity & Anti-Aging.title: The APOEε4 Variant Interferes in Myelination in the Aging Brain
Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: Of the common variants of the APOE gene, APOEε4 presents the greatest risk of Alzheimer's disease. APOE is involved in lipid metabolism, and APOEε4 is associated with lipid-related contributions to inflammation in microglia, suggesting a primarily inflammatory mechanism for the increased risk of neurodegeneration. Here, researchers find that APOEε4 also interferes in the ability of oligodendrocyte cells to maintain the myelin structures that sheath the axons that connect neurons into neural networks, again via lipid-related mechanisms. This myelin sheathing is required for effective communication between neurons. Longevity & Anti-Aging.title: Type 2 immunity as a counter-regulatory axis in aging
Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: Nature Aging, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s43587-026-01265-1Chronic low-grade inflammation is a hallmark of aging, but the endogenous programs that normally restrain it are far less understood than its drivers. Type 2 immunity is classically linked to allergy and anti-helminth defense, yet it also acts as a homeostatic circuit that preserves hematopoietic, macrophage and metabolic homeostasis. Here we argue that age-related erosion of this axis may contribute to inflammaging and represent a potential gerotherapeutic target for restoring immune homeostasis.
